clinicalPearls: An inherited disorder of dentine formation giving teeth an opalescent blue-grey to amber-brown discolouration, affecting both dentitions
The overlying enamel, though normal, is poorly supported and readily chips and shears away, exposing soft dentine to rapid attrition
Radiographs show bulbous crowns with cervical constriction and progressive obliteration of the pulp chambers and root canals
Type I occurs as part of osteogenesis imperfecta, whereas types II and III affect the teeth alone
It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and, in the isolated forms, is caused by mutations in the DSPP gene
The primary teeth are often more severely affected than the permanent teeth
Early, often generalised, tooth wear can lead to loss of occlusal vertical dimension
Management focuses on protecting teeth from wear with overlays, crowns, or overdentures and on preserving vertical dimension
reference.pathophysiology: Dentinogenesis imperfecta arises from defective dentine matrix: in the isolated forms owing to mutations in the dentine sialophosphoprotein (DSPP) gene, and when part of osteogenesis imperfecta owing to type I collagen defects shared with bone. The resulting dentine is abnormally structured and poorly mineralised, so it cannot adequately support the overlying enamel; the enamel-dentine junction is weak and the enamel fractures away, exposing dentine that then wears rapidly. Continued deposition of abnormal dentine within the pulp space produces the characteristic bulbous crowns and obliterated pulp chambers and canals.
additionalDifferentials: Osteogenesis imperfecta with dental involvement, defining type I
Congenital erythropoietic porphyria and other causes of intrinsic discolouration
Vitamin D-dependent or hypophosphataemic rickets affecting dentine
additionalInvestigations: Dental and family history with pedigree, including questions about fractures and blue sclerae
Clinical examination for opalescent discolouration and enamel loss in both dentitions
Radiographs demonstrating bulbous crowns, cervical constriction, and pulp obliteration
Assessment for systemic features of osteogenesis imperfecta with appropriate referral
Genetic testing (for example DSPP or collagen genes) where indicated
Study models and clinical photographs to plan restorative care and monitor wear
redFlags: Systemic features of osteogenesis imperfecta such as recurrent fractures, blue sclerae, or hearing loss
Rapid loss of tooth structure with collapse of the bite
Recurrent dental abscesses or difficult endodontics due to obliterated canals
Marked functional and aesthetic impairment in a child affecting wellbeing
reference.prognosis: With protective restorative management teeth can be preserved and function maintained, but severely affected teeth may wear down or fracture and ultimately require crowns, overdentures, or replacement; the systemic prognosis in type I depends on the associated osteogenesis imperfecta.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise the association with osteogenesis imperfecta and missing a systemic diagnosis
Confusing the condition with amelogenesis imperfecta or dentine dysplasia
Attempting routine endodontics without anticipating obliterated canals
Allowing progressive wear through delayed protective treatment
references: Cawson's Essentials of Oral Pathology and Oral Medicine
management: Provide protective restorative care to prevent enamel shearing and dentine wear, using preformed metal crowns on primary molars and full-coverage crowns or onlays on permanent teeth
Institute an intensive preventive regime with topical fluoride and meticulous oral hygiene
Rehabilitate established attrition with overdentures and occlusal restoration to maintain the vertical dimension of occlusion
Address the opalescent discolouration with crowns or veneers where aesthetics are a concern
Assess for associated osteogenesis imperfecta in type I and refer for bone management including bisphosphonate therapy
Monitor long-term with serial radiographs, study models and photographs within a paediatric dentistry and prosthodontics team
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance, with DSPP variants in the isolated forms
